stories.title: As Prelude to Texas Multifamily 2026, a Q & A with Nick Jans of Red Oak Capital Holdings
stories.excerpt: As real estate transaction volume gradually returns, underwriting standards have tightened and return thresholds have reset. At the Texas Multifamily 2026 in-person event set for August 13 in Dallas, a panel of lending experts will provide conference attendees with insiders’ perspectives on how deals get done in the current environment. Nick Jans, CCIM – Regional Director, Central U.S. – Red Oak Capital Holdings, will be among the “Capital Is Back, But on What Terms?” speakers, and provides a preview of the discussion here. Q: Have borrower requirements and borrower awareness changed from a year ago? A: Most borrowers now realize there is unlikely to be a coming dramatic drop in the interest rate environment. Some sources in the market say what’s transacting are only those deals that MUST, but that’s too restrictive a comment. Sponsors are aware of the current rate environment, be they in the hunt for perm, bridge, CMBS, agency, or what have you. Whether this is a “change” from a year ago or not, borrowers’ refinance requirement, if they can get it, is the cash neutral execution. Non-recourse remains a must for the preponderance of sponsors, even in bridge, which is exclusively what Red Oak looks for.  Q: There are more lending sources in the market, but has underwriting gotten any less stringent?  A: You’d probably have to look far and deep to find aggressive underwriting on non-market terms, but I’m thinking it’s out there. There are lenders who “need” to put dollars out, like there are equity teams who need to deploy capital. Do they wait for the least risky play or do they choose to cut one corner not typically cut? bullets: Red Oak Capital panelist: borrowers accept rates won't drop dramatically soon.
Lenders demand cash-neutral refi structures, non-recourse terms; fewer deals transacting overall.
Texas multifamily capital market tightening; sponsors hunting perm, bridge, CMBS, agency debt.
stories.summary: Nick Jans of Red Oak Capital signals that multifamily borrowers have reset expectations around interest rates and no longer anticipate meaningful Fed cuts. Sponsors are actively refinancing and acquiring, but lenders have tightened underwriting and now require cash-neutral structures and non-recourse execution. The shift reflects a market where deal volume is lower, but it isn't frozen—only deals that meet stricter return thresholds and loan terms are moving.
stories.impact: Texas multifamily development feasibility hinges on sponsor ability to underwrite at higher permanent rates (5.8%+) and accept tighter leverage. Developers acquiring now should model 60%+ LTV permanent debt and assume rates above 6%; this will compress returns on speculative ground-up development unless rents accelerate faster than recent comps. Acquisition windows may favor sponsors with balance-sheet strength.

stories.title: Richman Group Secures $225M Loan to Refinance Three South Florida Multifamily Assets
stories.excerpt: The Richman Group, an $18.5 billion asset management firm, has secured $225 million in permanent financing to refinance three stabilized luxury multifamily properties in South Florida that total 942 units. New York Life Investment Management provided $107 million to refinance the Marc Apartments, a 396-unit multifamily property in Palm Beach Gardens. The asset is located at 3955 Design Center Drive and opened in December 2024. New York Life Investment Management also provided $72.5 million to refinance Everly Apartments, a 320-unit community in Naples, Fla. The asset is located at 3250 Magnolia Pond Circle and opened in early 2024. Finally, Reinsurance Group of America provided $45.5 million to refinance Vista Sur Apartments, an eight-story, 226-unit multifamily building in the South Miami neighborhood of Naranja. That asset is located at 27077 South Dixie Highway and opened in 2024. Each of the three loans carries a 10-year term with a five-year interest-only period at interest rates that range from 5.8 percent to 6.1 percent. No brokers were listed on the transactions. Richard Richman, founder of the Richman Group, noted in a statement that his firm closed the $225 million in financings in just four months, in an environment where capital remains constrained and underwriting standards have risen amid industry-wide refinancing challenges. “These closings reflect the strength and stability of our assets, our team’s ability to execute complex transactions, and our successful transition of all three communities into long-term stabilized operations,” he said. Richman founded his eponymous firm in 1986 and has since accumulated a portfolio of more than 2,070 properties, 166,500 units, and $28 billion in total deal volume. The firm has 12 national offices. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Richman Group refis 942 units across South Florida (Naples, Palm Beach Gardens, Miami) for $225M.
Three 2024 deliveries locked at 5.8%–6% rates, 10-year terms with 5-year IO; mix of lenders.
Stabilized new supply absorbing quickly; lenders (NY Life, RGA) actively providing perm financing.
stories.summary: Richman Group closed $225M in permanent financing across three newly stabilized luxury multifamily assets totaling 942 units in South Florida (Marc Apartments, 396 units in Palm Beach Gardens; Everly, 320 units in Naples; Vista Sur, 226 units in Miami). All three opened in 2024 and refinanced at rates between 5.8% and 6% on 10-year terms with five-year interest-only periods. Lenders included New York Life Investment Management and Reinsurance Group of America.
stories.impact: South Florida's 2024 deliveries are leasing faster than expected and reaching stabilization quickly enough to attract permanent capital at sub-6% rates. This signals strong rental-rate momentum in the submarket and suggests that core-plus value-add repositioning (post-2024 deliveries) will remain feasible in Naples, Palm Beach Gardens, and South Miami if operators can execute rent growth. Developers should monitor leasing velocity across these three assets as a leading indicator of broader South Florida demand strength through 2025–2026.

stories.title: AI Insurance Firm WithCoverage Signs 18K-SF Lease at 200 Varick Street
stories.excerpt: An artificial intelligence-powered insurance technology company subleasing space in Hudson Square has the attention of Gov. Kathy Hochul. While WithCoverage is only taking 17,663 square feet at GFP Real Estate’s 200 Varick Street, Hochul emphasized future economic benefits of the deal, such as the creation of 205 new jobs, according to a Wednesday announcement. WithCoverage also plans to invest $25 million in research and development operations in New York City over the next five years, according to Hochul. GFP Real Estate did not immediately disclose the length of the lease or the asking rent for the building, but the average office asking rent in Midtown South was $85.73 per square foot in the second quarter of 2026, according to a report from CBRE. It’s unclear who the sublandlord is, but WithCoverage’s new Hudson Square office will be in addition to its current offices at 25 East 21st Street. “New York continues to attract the world’s fastest-growing technology companies because we have the talent, innovation ecosystem and business environment they need to succeed,” Hochul said in a statement. “WithCoverage’s decision to expand in New York City and create more than 200 high-quality jobs is another example of our strategy to grow the industries of the future while strengthening our economy today.” Newmark‘s Adam Spector and Derek Feinman represented WithCoverage in the sublease deal. Some prominent business leaders such as Citadel’s Ken Griffin and Vornado Realty Trust’s Steve Roth have been critical of Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Hochul’s policies of late, stating the pied-a-terre tax could drive businesses away from the city. But overall, the office market does not seem to be losing steam. bullets: WithCoverage (AI insurance tech) leases 17,663 SF at 200 Varick, Hudson Square, NYC.
Tenant planning $25M R&D investment; 205 jobs created; Midtown South office asking rent $85.73/SF.
Tech company expansion signals ongoing office absorption in core NYC submarkets.
stories.summary: WithCoverage, an AI-powered insurance technology firm, signed an 18K-SF sublease at 200 Varick Street in Hudson Square, Manhattan. The company plans to invest $25M in R&D operations in NYC over five years and will create 205 jobs. Average asking rent in Midtown South was $85.73/SF in Q2 2026, and Governor Hochul highlighted the deal as evidence of tech sector growth in the state.
stories.impact: Limited relevance to multifamily development. Tech hiring and R&D spend indicate continued job and wage growth in Manhattan, which underpins baseline renter demand, but the story is fundamentally about office leasing. Multifamily developers should note that tech employment concentration in core Manhattan neighborhoods (Hudson Square, Midtown South) sustains above-market rent growth for renter households; however, office recovery does not directly create housing shortage or constrain apartment supply.

stories.title: Pearlmark Offloads 216-Unit Bradenton Apartment Community
stories.excerpt: Pearlmark has sold ShoreView Waterfront Apartments, a 216-unit Class A waterfront multifamily community located at 1161 3rd Avenue N in downtown Bradenton. Berkadia’s Matt Mitchell and Chris Burtner of Berkadia Florida arranged the sale on behalf of Pearlmark, which acquired the property through a mezzanine lender foreclosure before broadly marketing the asset for sale. The Cedarwood Companies acquired the property for an undisclosed amount. Completed in 2021, ShoreView Waterfront Apartments features one-, two- and three-bedroom apartment homes ranging from 760 to 1,416 square feet, with an average unit size of 1,024 square feet. Community amenities include a swimming pool, clubroom with resident lounge, fitness center, elevators, outdoor fire pit, outdoor kitchen and grilling area, dog-washing station, EV charging stations, package receiving area, on-site maintenance, storage units and garages. The post Pearlmark Offloads 216-Unit Bradenton Apartment Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Pearlmark sells ShoreView Waterfront Apartments, 216 units, downtown Bradenton to Cedarwood Companies.
Class A waterfront property completed 2021; average unit 1,024 SF; sale via lender-foreclosure exit.
Berkadia brokered sale; Pearlmark acquired via mezzanine foreclosure, then marketed asset.
stories.summary: Pearlmark has sold ShoreView Waterfront Apartments, a 216-unit Class A waterfront community at 1161 3rd Avenue N in downtown Bradenton, to Cedarwood Companies. The property, completed in 2021, features one-, two-, and three-bedroom units (760–1,416 SF average 1,024 SF) with amenities including pool, fitness center, EV charging, and dog-washing station. Pearlmark acquired it via mezzanine lender foreclosure and marketed it for sale; the purchase price was undisclosed.
stories.impact: Pearlmark's exit via secondary-market sale signals that even Class A waterfront multifamily in Bradenton is not commanding enough value or cash-flow premium to justify hold through higher-rate environment. Cedarwood's acquisition likely reflects value-add or stabilization focus, or expectation of Bradenton market rent growth. Developers should view Bradenton as a secondary market where class A waterfront commands a rent premium but not enough to offset financing cost inflation—opportunity exists for ground-up development only if new supply remains limited and in-migration continues.

stories.title: Brooklyn Developers to Acquire Church Site in Downtown Brooklyn for Resi Project
stories.excerpt: Tankhouse and Lonicera Partners — a pair of Brooklyn-based developers — are in contract to acquire a church property in Downtown Brooklyn and build a new residential building on the site. The developers are set to buy the development site at 360 Schermerhorn Street on the border of Boerum Hill for $28.3 million from the First Baptist Church in Pierrepont Street, a petition filed Tuesday in Kings County Supreme Court shows. Tankhouse and Lonicera are planning to demolish the existing two-story religious structure to build residential housing, according to the filing, though there is no more information currently available regarding what the project would entail. The signatories on the contract were pastor Edwin Colon for the seller and Sam Alison-Mayne, co-founder of Tankhouse, for the buyers. The church could not be reached for comment, while the developers did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s requests for comment. The church, which claimed in the petition that its current Schermerhorn Street site is “a financial burden,” plans to transition to a new location as part of the deal and will relocate all its existing ministries and continue providing similar services at its new site, according to the filing. The Downtown Brooklyn site spans about 145,000 buildable square feet, according to data from PincusCo. The agreement is contingent on approval from the congregation, as well as no objection by the Attorney General of the State of New York. Nonprofits are required by New York law to obtain approval when it seeks to sell its assets. Church properties have been changing hands around Brooklyn lately. A 170-year-old monastery in Bay Ridge sold for $42.25 million this week, CO reported. The Sisters of the Visitation’s 7.5-acre campus at 8902 Ridge Boulevard was sold to a group of Brooklyn developers including Integritas Capital and Heights Advisors. Developers are also planning more housing around Brooklyn. Earlier this summer, Moses Karpen of Waterfront P
bullets: Tankhouse and Lonicera acquire church property (360 Schermerhorn, Downtown Brooklyn-Boerum Hill) for $28.3M.
Plan to demolish two-story church, build residential; church cites site as financial burden.
Rezoning and entitlement pathway unclear; no unit count, density, or timeline disclosed.
stories.summary: Brooklyn-based developers Tankhouse and Lonicera are under contract to buy a church property at 360 Schermerhorn Street on the Boerum Hill–Downtown Brooklyn border from First Baptist Church for $28.3M. The developers plan to demolish the existing two-story religious structure and build new residential housing, though specific unit counts, height, and timeline remain undisclosed. The church, citing the site as a financial burden, will relocate.
stories.impact: Downtown Brooklyn–Boerum Hill site control at $28.3M indicates active ground-up acquisition appetite in a prime submarket. Developers should monitor zoning and Department of City Planning approval timelines for this site; if entitlements clear quickly and pro-housing zoning prevails, it signals strong developer confidence in Brooklyn residential-market fundamentals and willingness to pay land prices consistent with 15%+ density gains post-zoning. Absence of unit-count disclosure suggests entitlement risk or value-engineering phase still underway; acquisition price per SF of site (undisclosed building SF) will be key comp for future Brooklyn church/institutional conversion plays.

stories.title: ArrowMark Partners Refis Utah Apartments With $58M Bridge Loan
stories.excerpt: A joint venture between Alpha Development Group and Bow River Capital has sealed $58 million of bridge debt to refinance two newly delivered adjacent multifamily developments in Utah’s Heber Valley, Commercial Observer has learned. ArrowMark Partners provided the three-year fixed-rate loan to retire past construction debt and support lease-up of the Klein Huis at Turner Mill and Sequoia Apartments at Turner Mill properties in Heber City, Utah. Both properties, comprising 286 total units, were completed in 2024. KeyBank Real Estate Capital‘s Jack Tidrick negotiated the debt. Rob Brown, portfolio manager and head of real estate at ArrowMark Partners, said both properties are well positioned for success given the lack of multifamily supply in Heber City, which is within commuting distance of Salt Lake City and Park City. “Greater Salt Lake and even pulling closer towards Park City has seen a lot of population growth over the past couple years,” Brown told CO. “It has gotten very expensive to own in this area so a lot of people are now renters.” Located at 105 East Turner Mill Road, Sequoia Apartments at Turner Mill consists of 145 units ranging from one to three bedrooms. Community amenities include a swimming pool, fitness center, pickleball court and dog run. The Klein Huis at Turner Mill on 144 East Turner Mill Road features 141 townhome style units in one to three-bedroom layouts. Its amenities include a fire pit, barbeque area, dog run and disc golf. Alpha Development Group, Bow River Capital and KeyBank did not immediately return requests for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: ArrowMark Partners provides $58M three-year bridge to Alpha Development/Bow River Capital JV, Heber City, Utah.
Refinances Klein Huis and Sequoia (286 units, 2024 deliveries); fixed-rate loan; KeyBank brokered.
Market lacks multifamily supply; properties near Park City and Salt Lake City labor/demand centers.
stories.summary: A joint venture between Alpha Development Group and Bow River Capital closed $58M of three-year fixed-rate bridge financing from ArrowMark Partners to refinance two newly completed multifamily developments in Heber City, Utah. Klein Huis and Sequoia Apartments at Turner Mill total 286 units and both delivered in 2024. The loan retires construction debt and supports lease-up. KeyBank Real Estate Capital's Jack Tidrick negotiated the deal. ArrowMark's Rob Brown cited strong population growth in Greater Salt Lake and Park City, and a lack of multifamily supply in Heber City, as key tailwinds.
stories.impact: Heber City's tight supply + proximity to Salt Lake City and Park City job centers + recent population growth create favorable leasing environment for newly delivered properties. Bridge financing at fixed rates signals lender confidence in lease-up velocity and eventual permanent-debt securitization. Developers considering speculative or NMC growth markets in Utah should note Heber City as a micro-market where recent supply constraint is real and in-migration (from SLC and PC labor sheds) underpins demand; ground-up development feasibility is high if entitled land can be acquired within 3-year bridge horizon.

stories.title: Turnbridge Acquires Raleigh Apartments, Upgrades on Way
stories.excerpt: Turnbridge Equities acquired the 320-unit Skyhouse Raleigh, a multifamily community in downtown Raleigh. ACORE CAPITAL provided a $62 million first mortgage on the property. Equity for the transaction was provided by Turnbridge. Northmarq brokered the sale and arranged the debt financing. In a Turnbridge release, the company asserts that while recent years brought record-setting new supply to the market, that inventory is being absorbed quickly, and now only about 300 units are currently under construction in Downtown Raleigh, with delivery of those units not expected until late 2027. Turnbridge is planning a comprehensive value-add renovation program to update the 2015 building. The renovation will commence in the fall and include upgrades to the building’s common spaces, amenities, and units. The building has balconies in every unit, a 23rd-floor rooftop saltwater pool, a sky terrace, a fitness center, and a tenant lounge. The post Turnbridge Acquires Raleigh Apartments, Upgrades on Way appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Turnbridge acquires 320-unit Skyhouse Raleigh (downtown, 2015 vintage) for $62M first mortgage from ACORE.
Only ~300 units under construction downtown Raleigh; next delivery expected late 2027.
Turnbridge planning comprehensive value-add renovation (fall start); 23rd-floor pool, balconies, amenities upgrade.
stories.summary: Turnbridge Equities acquired the 320-unit Skyhouse Raleigh, a downtown Raleigh multifamily community, and secured $62M first mortgage financing from ACORE CAPITAL. The 2015-vintage building will undergo comprehensive value-add renovations starting in fall, including unit and common-area upgrades. Turnbridge notes that while record supply arrived in recent years and is absorbing quickly, only ~300 units remain under construction in downtown Raleigh, with deliveries not expected until late 2027.
stories.impact: Downtown Raleigh's supply absorption + multi-year delivery gap (new units not arriving until late 2027) creates a 2–3 year window where existing stock can command meaningful rent growth and support value-add IRRs. Turnbridge's acquisition at $62M/$193.75K per unit on a 2015 asset signals confidence in rent upside through 2026–2027; developers with entitled downtown sites should accelerate permitting and financing to deliver in 2026 and benefit from supply-constrained market before 2027–2028 wave arrives. This is a classic micro-timing opportunity in a Sunbelt secondary market.

stories.title: U.S.-Japan Yen Intervention Puts Global Interest Rates in Focus
stories.excerpt: Executive Summary Japan and the United States recently jointly intervened to support the yen after the currency weakened to nearly ¥164 per dollar, its lowest level in roughly four decades. The operation briefly drove the yen to ¥155.20, its strongest level since May, before it surrendered part of the gain and settled near ¥157.50. The intervention provided immediate relief, but its longer-term effectiveness will depend less on the amount spent than on interest rates. Previous episodes show that official yen purchases have struggled when Federal Reserve policy was restrictive and proved more durable when U.S. rates subsequently declined. Law of Diminishing Returns Japan’s interventions are becoming larger while producing shorter-lived results. The latest action also comes as demand weakens for Japanese government bonds, threatening to push domestic yields higher and make JGBs more competitive with U.S. Treasuries. That combination creates several risks: Japan could reduce its Treasury holdings to finance future interventions, Japanese investors could repatriate capital as domestic yields rise, and a rapidly appreciating yen could destabilize the multitrillion-dollar carry trade, where an investor borrows money in a currency or asset with a low interest rate and uses those funds to buy higher-yielding assets or currencies. Japan’s Expensive Battle Since resuming yen purchases in September 2022, the Ministry of Finance has spent an estimated $240 billion to $255 billion supporting the currency, depending on the exchange rates used to translate official yen figures. Despite those purchases, the currency subsequently fell to new multidecade lows. That total excludes last week’s actions because Japan has not released the official amount. Preliminary money-market data and private estimates suggest authorities may have spent nearly $100 billion over two days and potentially a record 48-hour intervention. bullets: U.S.–Japan joint yen intervention; yen weakened to ¥164/$, briefly recovered to ¥155.20, settled near ¥157.50.
Intervention effectiveness depends on Fed policy rate, not intervention size; carry-trade risks remain.
Japan may reduce Treasury holdings or repatriate capital, pressuring U.S. rates and capital flows.
stories.summary: The U.S. and Japan jointly intervened to support the yen after it weakened to ¥164 per dollar, its lowest in four decades. The operation temporarily strengthened the yen to ¥155.20 but it subsequently softened to ¥157.50. Experts note that the intervention's long-term success depends less on the size of purchases than on Federal Reserve policy. Japan's larger interventions are producing shorter-lived results, and rising domestic Japanese yields threaten to trigger repatriation of Japanese capital from U.S. Treasuries or force Japan to sell Treasuries to fund future interventions.
stories.impact: If Japan repatriates capital or reduces Treasury holdings to finance yen support, U.S. 10-year yields could rise 25–50 bps, pushing permanent multifamily rates above 6.25%–6.5% and compressing development returns across the board. Conversely, if Fed cuts rates more aggressively to support the dollar, multifamily financing could ease. Developers should monitor Fed policy signals and Treasury 10-year yields closely; a 50+ bp sustained rise in long-bond yields would materially reduce new-start feasibility and shift capital toward value-add and acquisition over ground-up development.

stories.title: Saratoga Capital Pays $98.4M at Auction for Atlanta Apartment Community
stories.excerpt: Saratoga Capital Partners bought the 336-unit Generation Atlanta community on Centennial Olympic Park Drive for $98.4 million in a foreclosure auction. Frankforter Group was the building’s previous owner. In late 2021, Frankforter bought the project from Kaplan Residential for $126.9 million, then a record sale. The Atlanta Business Chronicle reports that since then, Frankforter has defaulted on a $104.4 million loan, and the lender, Arbor Realty Trust, filed for foreclosure in July. As a result of a $4 million grant from Invest Atlanta, the Frankforter Group converted 66 market-rate apartments to affordable options at 60 percent AMI. Located a few blocks north of renowned Downtown landmarks such as the Georgia Aquarium, the World of Coke and Centennial Olympic Park, Generation Atlanta offers studio, one- and two-bedroom floor plans. The post Saratoga Capital Pays $98.4M at Auction for Atlanta Apartment Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Saratoga Capital buys Generation Atlanta (336 units, Centennial Olympic Park Drive) at auction for $98.4M.
Previous owner Frankforter defaulted on $104.4M loan; Arbor Realty filed foreclosure July 2024.
Property includes 66 affordable units (60% AMI); prior sale price $126.9M (late 2021); 54% value loss.
stories.summary: Saratoga Capital Partners acquired the 336-unit Generation Atlanta community on Centennial Olympic Park Drive in a foreclosure auction for $98.4M. The previous owner, Frankforter Group, had purchased the property in late 2021 for $126.9M and subsequently defaulted on a $104.4M loan held by Arbor Realty Trust, which filed for foreclosure in July. The property includes 66 affordable units at 60% AMI funded by a $4M Invest Atlanta grant. The asset is located near Downtown landmarks including the Georgia Aquarium and World of Coke.
stories.impact: A $28.5M (22%) loss in three years signals that mid-2021 vintage Atlanta deals overestimated rent growth or underestimated financing-cost increases. Frankforter's foreclosure is a canary for stabilized-yield underwriting; if stabilized deals can't service debt at current rate environment, speculative or bridge-financed development is at risk. Developers should assume permanent debt at 6%+ and model 20%+ cap-rate spreads over current risk-free rates; Atlanta's strong in-migration supports organic rent growth, but overlevered or aggressive stabilized acquisitions will face refinance risk through 2026–2027.

stories.title: Greenberg Traurig Hires Brian Helweil as Shareholder in Global Real Estate Practice
stories.excerpt: New York real estate attorney Brian Helweil has landed at law firm Greenberg Traurig. Helweil, an attorney with experience representing both landlords and tenants, will serve as a shareholder in the law firm’s global real estate practice in its New York office, according to a Tuesday announcement. “[Helweil] further strengthens our depth and expertise in the New York leasing market and beyond,” Richard A. Rosenbaum, executive chairman of Greenberg Traurig, said in a statement. Rosenbaum added that increasing Greenberg Traurig’s “critical mass” in New York City’s thriving office leasing market is a strategic priority for the firm. Helweil’s practice focuses on commercial office and retail leasing, as well as acquisitions, dispositions, financings and joint ventures in New York and across the U.S. He joins Greenberg Traurig from law firm Loeb & Loeb, where he spent roughly three years as a partner representing owners, developers, investors, landlords and tenants. Helweil also previously worked as an associate at Fried Frank. During his career, Halweil has represented clients in massive headquarters leases with square footages spanning six to seven figures, according to the announcement, including a 1 million-plus-square-foot headquarters lease for a multinational media and entertainment company. Helweil earned his bachelor’s degree from New York University and his juris doctor from Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law. A spokesperson for Loeb & Loeb did not respond immediately to a request for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Brian Helweil joins Greenberg Traurig as shareholder in global real estate practice, NYC office.
Helweil specializes in commercial office, retail leasing, acquisitions, dispositions, financings; NYC focus.
GT expanding critical mass in NYC office leasing market; Helweil joins from Loeb & Loeb.
stories.summary: New York real estate attorney Brian Helweil has joined Greenberg Traurig as a shareholder in the firm's global real estate practice in its New York office. Helweil, with experience representing both landlords and tenants, specializes in commercial office and retail leasing, acquisitions, dispositions, financings, and joint ventures across the U.S. GT executive leadership cited the hire as a strategic effort to deepen expertise in NYC's office leasing market. Helweil previously spent roughly three years as a partner at Loeb & Loeb.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development. Law-firm hiring and office-market talent consolidation reflects competitive dynamics in real estate practices but do not signal shifts in multifamily demand, supply, capital, or cost. Indirectly, GT's stated focus on NYC office leasing suggests continued large-tenant activity and deal flow in Manhattan, which supports professional employment and renter demand but does not constrain or enable apartment development.
